canonical_definition:
What it is. Across the papers, BoolQ is most commonly described as a yes/no question-answering benchmark or dataset, typically with a question paired with a passage or short context and a binary answer, and often framed as reading comprehension or commonsense reasoning. Several definitions add that the questions are natural or naturally occurring and unprompted; some descriptions say the questions are about Wikipedia articles, and one paper describes BoolQ as a closed-book QA dataset. One paper spells out the format and size, stating that each example has a question, a passage, and a binary answer, with 15942 examples split into train, validation, and test.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use BoolQ to measure a broad range of targets rather than a single one: it is linked to 9 constructs and 10 behavioral indicators. The prevailing construct-level framing is commonsense reasoning, and other recurring uses frame it as measuring machine reading comprehension, question answering, reasoning, and language understanding task performance. The remaining links are spread across additional construct and task framings, so papers do not present a single exclusive measurement claim.

Space of uses. Most papers present BoolQ as one task within broader evaluation suites, often in zero-shot settings and sometimes in few-shot or 32-shot evaluation. It is linked to 4 other instruments: papers most often place it within SuperGLUE or report results through lm-evaluation-harness, and smaller lines of work include it in OLMES or relate it to Commonsense170K. Some papers also use it as a source task, warm-up QA data, a held-out generalization test, or part of calibration and self-correction evaluations.

Concerns raised. Concern-focused use appears in contamination studies: papers use BoolQ to measure benchmark overfitting and to evaluate the impact of data contamination alongside other benchmarks.

characterization_sections.label: What it is.
characterization_sections.text: Across the papers, BoolQ is most commonly described as a yes/no question-answering benchmark or dataset, typically with a question paired with a passage or short context and a binary answer, and often framed as reading comprehension or commonsense reasoning. Several definitions add that the questions are natural or naturally occurring and unprompted; some descriptions say the questions are about Wikipedia articles, and one paper describes BoolQ as a closed-book QA dataset. One paper spells out the format and size, stating that each example has a question, a passage, and a binary answer, with 15942 examples split into train, validation, and test.

characterization_sections.label: What it is claimed to measure.
characterization_sections.text: Papers use BoolQ to measure a broad range of targets rather than a single one: it is linked to 9 constructs and 10 behavioral indicators. The prevailing construct-level framing is commonsense reasoning, and other recurring uses frame it as measuring machine reading comprehension, question answering, reasoning, and language understanding task performance. The remaining links are spread across additional construct and task framings, so papers do not present a single exclusive measurement claim.

characterization_sections.label: Space of uses.
characterization_sections.text: Most papers present BoolQ as one task within broader evaluation suites, often in zero-shot settings and sometimes in few-shot or 32-shot evaluation. It is linked to 4 other instruments: papers most often place it within SuperGLUE or report results through lm-evaluation-harness, and smaller lines of work include it in OLMES or relate it to Commonsense170K. Some papers also use it as a source task, warm-up QA data, a held-out generalization test, or part of calibration and self-correction evaluations.

characterization_sections.label: Concerns raised.
characterization_sections.text: Concern-focused use appears in contamination studies: papers use BoolQ to measure benchmark overfitting and to evaluate the impact of data contamination alongside other benchmarks.

characterization:
What it is. Across the papers, BoolQ is most commonly described as a yes/no question-answering benchmark or dataset, typically with a question paired with a passage or short context and a binary answer, and often framed as reading comprehension or commonsense reasoning. Several definitions add that the questions are natural or naturally occurring and unprompted; some descriptions say the questions are about Wikipedia articles, and one paper describes BoolQ as a closed-book QA dataset. One paper spells out the format and size, stating that each example has a question, a passage, and a binary answer, with 15942 examples split into train, validation, and test.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use BoolQ to measure a broad range of targets rather than a single one: it is linked to 9 constructs and 10 behavioral indicators. The prevailing construct-level framing is commonsense reasoning, and other recurring uses frame it as measuring machine reading comprehension, question answering, reasoning, and language understanding task performance. The remaining links are spread across additional construct and task framings, so papers do not present a single exclusive measurement claim.

Space of uses. Most papers present BoolQ as one task within broader evaluation suites, often in zero-shot settings and sometimes in few-shot or 32-shot evaluation. It is linked to 4 other instruments: papers most often place it within SuperGLUE or report results through lm-evaluation-harness, and smaller lines of work include it in OLMES or relate it to Commonsense170K. Some papers also use it as a source task, warm-up QA data, a held-out generalization test, or part of calibration and self-correction evaluations.

Concerns raised. Concern-focused use appears in contamination studies: papers use BoolQ to measure benchmark overfitting and to evaluate the impact of data contamination alongside other benchmarks.
